AI agents: set-up in VS Code with GitHub Copilot

Source: vignettes/articles/ai-agents-vscode-copilot.Rmd
ai-agents-vscode-copilot.Rmd

In Japanese

This page sets up VS Code with GitHub Copilot’s agent for work on rtfreporter, tflspec or tflplanner. Read Developing with AI agents first: it says what the set-up is for. Come back to that page for the workflow when you are done.

The facts here come from the VS Code and GitHub documentation, read on 2026-11-08 (see the links). None of the steps was run in VS Code for this page. Copilot’s screens and settings change often. If a step does not match what you see, read the linked page again.

Open the repository

  1. Clone the repository. A contributor clones a fork. A maintainer (a Collaborator) clones ichirio/rtfreporter (Contributor vs Collaborator in CONTRIBUTING.md). CONTRIBUTING.md also shows the VS Code Source Control route.
  2. Open the folder in VS Code (File > Open Folder…).
  3. Make the topic branch from the right base: run Git: Create Branch… from the Command Palette. A contributor branches from main and opens the pull request against main; a maintainer’s branch goes to next (Branching & collaboration in CONTRIBUTING.md). AGENTS.md, which Copilot’s instructions point to, names main only, so a maintainer follows CONTRIBUTING.md.
  4. In the chat input, select Agent from the agent picker. The documentation names a Local harness and a Copilot harness. It says the Local harness is deprecated and will be removed in February 2027, and it advises moving to the Copilot harness. But prompt files run only in the Local harness (see the pre-PR check below).

Sources: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/sourcecontrol/overview, https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/sourcecontrol/branches-worktrees, https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/agents/agent-tools

The environment

The agent’s commands must see the work library and the work home, not yours (section 2 of the shared article).

  • In a Local session the agent runs commands in the integrated terminal; a Copilot harness session uses a built-in shell tool by default (the agent-tools page). Start VS Code from a shell where the variables are set (R_LIBS_USER, HOME, R_USER_CACHE_DIR, R_USER_DATA_DIR, R_USER_CONFIG_DIR, TMP, TEMP, TMPDIR, WORK_ROOT), so that every terminal inherits them. VS Code can also set variables for its terminals in terminal.integrated.env.windows, .osx or .linux (the terminal profiles page). The documentation does not say whether the agent’s terminal reads it, so run the check script to find out.
  • Tell the agent which R to call, by its full path, in the instruction file (next section).

Then ask the agent to run the check script from the shared article. The agent has not read the article, so paste the script into the chat first, and then write:

Save the script above as check-env.R outside the repository, run it with the project’s R, and show me the output.

It must end with Environment OK. If it stops, fix the environment first.

Instructions

Copilot in VS Code reads .github/copilot-instructions.md or AGENTS.md. This repository has both. .github/copilot-instructions.md already points to AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and the AI developer manual, and it already says that a pull request never edits NEWS.md, CHANGELOG.md or Version:. So keep it short and keep the rules in one place. Add only the lines that are missing:

- Call R by its full path (the project's R), never a bare `Rscript`.
- After the `pre-pr` prompt file below is added, run it (`/pre-pr`) before you open a pull request.
- Stop and ask before you push, install into any library other than the work library, or delete files.

.github/copilot-instructions.md is a tracked file, so a line you add lands in your pull request. Add a line only if it helps every contributor, and say so in the pull request. Instructions that are only for you go under User in the Agent Customizations editor. In the Copilot harness they are in ~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md or in ~/.copilot/instructions/. In the Local harness they are kept in your VS Code user profile. The instructions reference page describes both.

To confirm that the file was read:

  • Run Chat: Open Customizations from the Command Palette and select Instructions. The file should be listed. This shows that it was found, not that the agent followed it.
  • Start a new chat and look at the References section of the answer, where it is shown.
  • Read the changes and the tool activity to see whether the rules were followed.

Sources: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/custom-instructions, https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/configure-custom-instructions/add-repository-instructions

Permissions

The agent asks for approval before it runs a tool. In the approval prompt you can choose Allow Once. The terminal setting chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove holds rules that approve a command without asking. Each rule is true (approve), false (ask) or a regular expression between / characters. For this work, in your user or workspace settings:

{
  "chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove": {
    "/^git (status|diff|log)\\b/": true,
    "git push": false,
    "rm": false
  }
}

Three things from the documentation. A compound command is approved only if every part matches a true rule. A false rule makes VS Code ask; it does not block the command. And the page calls the rules “a best-effort convenience, not a security boundary”, so keep the work area apart from your own files, as in the environment section.

Keep these as “ask”: git push, installing into any library other than the work library, and deleting files. The approvals page does not say how a rule matches a command that is given by its full path, so test any rule for the project’s R before you rely on it. This article’s own advice: a rule that allows Rscript lets the agent run any R code, so add it only after the environment check passes.

Source: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/approvals

The pre-PR check

A prompt file is a Markdown file named <name>.prompt.md. A workspace prompt file lives in .github/prompts/. You start it by typing /<name> in the chat input, or with Chat: Run Prompt in the Command Palette. It runs only in Local harness sessions in the Chat view. The Local harness is deprecated and will be removed in February 2027, and the Copilot harness does not run a prompt file; for that harness the documentation suggests a skill instead. The example below therefore works only in the deprecated Local harness. This page does not show a skill for the Copilot harness, and the repository has no Copilot file for it. A Copilot skill example may come later. This example is .github/prompts/pre-pr.prompt.md:

Run these in order. Stop at the first failure and report it.

1. Run the tests of the changed area.
2. Run `lintr::lint_package()`. It must report 0 lints.
3. List the `pkg::` uses and `requireNamespace()` calls added in the diff, and
   check each is declared in `DESCRIPTION`.
4. When a change in tflspec can break tflplanner, run tflplanner's tests too.
5. Report each result in the pull request description, in the form the pull request template asks for.

Do not edit `NEWS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md` or `Version:`.

A prompt file may start with front matter. All of its fields are optional: description, name, argument-hint, agent (ask, agent, plan or a custom agent), model and tools. There is no mode field. The example needs none; add agent: agent to pin the agent that runs it.

This is a faster subset for each change, not the four pre-push checks of CONTRIBUTING.md (R CMD check --as-cran, devtools::test(), pkgdown::check_pkgdown() and lintr). CI runs the full set, and so does a maintainer before a release.

Source: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/prompt-files

Checks on each edit

VS Code has hooks, in Preview. A hook is a command that runs at a fixed point. Workspace hooks are JSON files in .github/hooks/. The event names are preToolUse and postToolUse. A preToolUse hook blocks a call by returning permissionDecision set to "deny"; a postToolUse hook cannot undo an action that has finished. A preToolUse hook that fails on an error denies the call, but a timeout falls through to the normal permissions. The rule “refuse an edit to NEWS.md or to Version:” would be one preToolUse hook.

A hook file has this shape (the command is a placeholder):

{
  "version": 1,
  "hooks": {
    "preToolUse": [
      { "type": "command", "command": "<your script>", "timeoutSec": 10 }
    ]
  }
}

The script gets toolName and toolArgs as input. To deny, it prints permissionDecision set to "deny" with a permissionDecisionReason; {} means no decision. A PascalCase event name such as PreToolUse is an alias that uses snake_case fields and Claude-style tool names (Read, Write, Edit). GitHub’s hooks reference says a matcher is a regular expression that must match the whole toolName, and that the file tools are edit and create (Edit and Write for the PascalCase alias). A hook for file edits would use the matcher edit|create. The VS Code hooks page says the Local harness ignores matcher values. Because the feature is in Preview, rely on the pre-PR check and on CI for these rules until you have tested a hook yourself.

The example hooks in .claude/ in the repository are written for Claude Code and tested only with it. They are in next now, and they reach main with the next merge. See the Claude app page.

Source: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/hooks

Then

Back to the workflow in the shared article: issue, small branch, test first, pre-PR check, pull request. To read an Issue or a pull request, the safe route is the GitHub CLI (gh) in the terminal. The VS Code pages read for this page do not say how Copilot reads an Issue or a pull request.

To hand a piece of work to a helper, VS Code has subagents: helpers that work in their own context and return a focused result. A subagent does not inherit the conversation, so state the goal, the files and the result you expect. Source: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/agents/subagents
